title: Rename a branch, delete the wrong one, get it back
summary: Branch housekeeping: rename to match the ticket, delete what is merged, refuse to delete what is not — and recover the one you deleted anyway.
mental_model: Deleting a branch deletes a name, not commits. If the commits were merged, they live on in the target branch. If they were not, they are unreachable but still in the object database — and the reflog remembers where the name pointed.

commit.message: Flesh out the state machine sketch

steps.title: Survey the branches
steps.why: `-vv` shows each branch, its tip and its upstream. Two feature branches, one badly named, one experimental. This is the normal state of any repository after a fortnight.

steps.title: Rename a branch to something meaningful
steps.why: `-m` renames. `feature/thing` tells a reviewer nothing; `feature/ABH-101-dosing` tells them the ticket and the subject. Renaming a local branch costs nothing and is never destructive.

steps.title: Ask which branches are safe to delete
steps.why: `--merged` lists branches whose commits are already contained in the current branch. Anything listed can be deleted with no loss. This is the query to run before any cleanup.
steps.expect: Both feature branches are --no-merged: their work is not in main yet.

steps.title: Merge one, then delete it safely
steps.why: After merging, the branch appears under `--merged` and `-d` removes it without argument. The commits survive inside main; only the label is gone.

verify.label: the merged work is in main

steps.title: Watch git refuse to delete unmerged work
steps.why: `-d` on the experimental branch fails, loudly, and tells you the sha. This refusal is one of git's best safety features — it only lets you lose work if you insist.
steps.expect: error: the branch is not fully merged. Exit code 1 is the point.

steps.title: Insist, and lose it
steps.why: `-D` is `--delete --force`. The name is gone and the two commits are now unreachable — `git log --all` cannot see them at all.
steps.expect: No trace of the state machine commits anywhere in --all.

steps.title: Recover the deleted branch
steps.why: The reflog holds every position HEAD has held, including commits that now belong to no branch. `git log -g` walks the reflog as if it were history, so you can search it by message instead of counting entries by eye.

verify.label: the deleted branch is back with both commits
verify.hint: find the tip sha in git reflog, then git branch <name> <sha>

verify.label: the merged feature branch was cleaned up
…and its work is safely inside main
the force-deleted branch was recovered from the reflog

pitfalls: `git branch -d` refuses unmerged branches relative to the branch you are standing on. Standing somewhere else changes the answer.
Renaming a branch that has an upstream leaves the old remote branch behind. Push the new name and delete the old one on the server explicitly.
`git branch -D` is the only common command that can silently orphan work. The reflog is your net, and it is not infinite.
`git fetch --prune` clears remote-tracking branches for branches deleted on the server; without it `git branch -r` accumulates ghosts.
cheatsheet: recreate a branch at any commit
